key_insight: Fewer than 2% of FDA-authorized AI medical devices are prognostic, and those that are span prediction horizons from minutes to years — signaling a small but diverse and growing category that raises distinct regulatory and ethical issues.
problem_solved: Documents the scarcity and variability of prognostic AI devices among FDA approvals and highlights the need to clarify regulatory pathways and ethical safeguards as these tools become more common.
method: Survey and categorization of FDA-authorized AI/ML medical devices to identify which are prognostic versus non-prognostic
Characterization of prediction horizons for prognostic devices (minutes → years) and synthesis of regulatory and ethical considerations
Discussion of implications for oversight, reporting standards, and developer responsibilities
impact: Alerts AI/ML practitioners that prognostic models are currently rare but heterogeneous, so development should anticipate specific regulatory requirements, transparent horizon reporting, and proactive ethical safeguards to enable safe deployment.
visual_elements: Pie chart: proportion of FDA-authorized devices that are prognostic (<2%) vs non-prognostic
Horizontal timeline or range bars: distribution of prediction horizons (minutes to years) for prognostic devices
Flowchart/checklist: regulatory and ethical decision pathway for developing and submitting prognostic AI
Icons: FDA/approval stamp, clock/calendar (prediction horizon), shield (ethics/safety), and an algorithm/brain symbol
paper_title: Authorization of prognostic AI medical devices
paper_authors: Urs J. Muehlematter, Kerstin Noelle Vokinger
